title: Semi Holdings Latest Earnings Scorecard
as_of: Figures as of 29–30 Oct 2026 unless marked live
summary: What the Global X Semiconductor ETF has done, what forecasters expect, what it holds, and the risks for a pension-age investor already heavy in TSLA, BTC and MSTR. General information only, not personal advice.

children: SEMI is a well-run, low-cost fund, but it is a single-sector, high-swing bet on the AI chip boom. It fell into a sharp sell-off in October, and it would add more of the same tech risk Bob already carries in TSLA, BTC and MSTR. General information only, not advice.

children: The 7.35% yield is not a steady income figure. It is driven by the large July 2026 payout (about 8% of the unit price), which looks like a one-off capital-gains distribution after a big year. Earlier half-year payouts were mostly 3–4 cents.

Global X figures to 29 Oct 2026, NAV total return in A$ after fees. The index did 0.6–0.7 points a year better, which is about the fee plus costs. These numbers don't yet include the US sell-off of Friday 30 Oct, when the US chip index fell 7.2% after the ASX had closed.
Calculated from SEMI.AX daily prices (yfinance) to 29 Oct 2026, using the same start dates. Gap column compares the last calculation to the site; ⚑ marks gaps over 0.5 points.

items: Price only is far below the site for 1 year and longer because it leaves out the big 2025 and 2026 payouts. That is expected, not an error.
The site uses NAV, not the ASX price. On 29 Oct the ASX close was A$34.98 against NAV of A$35.25, so ending at NAV adds about 0.8 points.
The 1-month, 3-month, YTD and 1-year gaps remain because the start-date ASX price also sat above or below NAV that day. Short periods magnify this.
The 3-year, 5-year and since-inception figures match within about 0.6 points, so the site's long-run CAGR figures check out.
30 Oct: US chip index (SOX) fell 7.2% and ended October down more than 15%. The Nasdaq fell 2.9% and the Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5%.
Intel fell 28.6%, its worst day since the 1970s, on weak Q4 guidance and a PC slump it expects to last through the first half of 2027.
AMD fell 10.9%, Qualcomm about 11%, Broadcom more than 5%, Micron 5.3% and Nvidia 4.2%.
Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft plan more than US$740bn of capex this year. Alphabet (−US$9.1bn) and Amazon reported negative free cash flow.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF is 29% off its high, which puts it in a bear market. BTIG's technical analyst recommended fading chip bounces.
Coming up: AMD results 3 Nov, the end of the US 'affiliates rule' suspension on 9 Nov, Nvidia results 17 Nov, and the WSTS autumn forecast on 1 Dec.

children: Because the ASX closed before Friday's US trading, SEMI may open lower on Monday 2 Nov.

pros: Nvidia, Broadcom, TSMC, Micron and SK Hynix all guided higher for the next quarter.
Micron and SK Hynix say memory stays tight through 2027–28, with most supply already contracted.
ASML, Lam and KLA expect 2027 equipment spending above US$200bn.
Gartner expects AI data centres to grow from 36.5% of chip revenue to 53% by 2030.
cons: Hyperscaler capex now partly relies on borrowing, and investors want to see returns.
Memory is about 54% of 2026 chip revenue, and it is the most boom-and-bust segment.
The low forward P/E rests on peak margins. Micron at about 6x shows investors don't trust those margins.
PC and phone demand is falling as memory costs rise. Intel expects PCs to drop 12% in 2026 and 10% in 2027.

sections.heading: Is a high CAGR likely over 2 years?

blocks.lead: Judgement: possible, but not the likely case
children: A repeat of the 56% a year of the last three years is unlikely. A more realistic range over 2 years runs from a loss to a moderate gain. The sourced forecasts point to modest positive returns on average, with a real chance of a 20–30% fall along the way.

items: Assumption: share prices follow earnings, and earnings follow industry revenue. WSTS and Gartner see about 25–27% revenue growth in 2027, after roughly doubling in 2026, so growth is slowing.

Assumption: valuations stay around today's 17x forward P/E. If they do, returns roughly track earnings growth. If investors treat this as a memory-cycle peak, multiples shrink, as they did from 21.7x in August.

Ocean Capital's 12-month SOX scenarios: base case +8% to +20% (55% chance), bull +31% to +45% (15%), bear −21% to −32% (30%). These are one firm's estimates, not consensus, and were made before the 30 Oct drop.
Unhedged A$ returns also depend on the exchange rate, which no one can forecast reliably.
Nothing here is a promise. Past performance is not a reliable guide to future returns.

rows.title: Age Pension and deeming
rows.detail: SEMI counts as a financial asset for Centrelink. Its value counts in the assets test and deeming sets the assumed income, so big swings change assessed assets. Distributions are also taxable, and lumpy

rows.title: Distribution yield misleading
rows.detail: 7.35% is mostly a one-off July payout, not reliable income

pros: Low 0.45% fee, A$995m in assets, and tracks its index closely.
Holds all 30 leaders across design, manufacturing, equipment and memory in one ASX trade.
Strong record: 34% a year over 5 years and 56% a year over 3 years.
Most top holdings just beat forecasts and guided higher.
Sector forward P/E is back near its long-run average after the October drop.
No Tesla, Bitcoin or MSTR inside, so the specific companies don't overlap.
cons: Strong past returns came from an exceptional boom.
Without hedging, the Aussie dollar can cut returns.
One sector, so it moves together in sell-offs.
